Wow, reading comprehension. He did NOT say "donating to charity is net negative." Did you even listen to the clip?

He says, very clearly, "I have my money in a donor-advised fund (DAF) and I try to put money towards things I think are helping civilization."

What is a DAF? A DAF is a charitable vehicle managed directly by a donor that CAN ONLY DONATE TO 501C(3) CHARITIES. A DAF is not a slush fund that you can use to invest into your friends' startups, you have to donate the money to an accredited nonprofit.

He is not criticizing "charity" in this clip. He is criticizing "Philanthropy" (capital P) in the form of self-perpetuating foundations made in their founder's names, which, he argues, only exist to keep existing, and ultimately lose sight of their original missions.

He criticizes SOME charities as being ideological and counterproductive (he alludes to the famous case of Scared Straight programs, which were found to actually increase rates of criminality). But that's not the same as saying "donating to all charity is negative." He just wants to make the decision for himself, rather than deferring to a foundation staffed by nonprofit drones.

He's still donating to charities, just ones he chooses. That's what a DAF is versus a foundation.

If you're looking for a "don't donate to charity" clip, or even a "billionaires are evil" clip, you picked the wrong one.

Can China train frontier models at scale on domestic hardware?

China can already run competitive AI models on domestic hardware, but it still has not demonstrated a frontier-scale training run using a fully domestic stack.

Frontier training requires thousands of accelerators to work together reliably at scale. That coordination depends on fast connections between chips, sufficient memory and stable software. A weakness anywhere in the system can stop the run.

China still relies on Nvidia stockpiles and approved imports for frontier training while Huawei develops domestic infrastructure around Ascend. Bringing that infrastructure to scale will also require more chip output from SMIC and continued progress in domestic memory and networking.

The 2027–28 model generation is the first that could plausibly be trained on Huawei’s domestic infrastructure. A fully disclosed training run would confirm that China can train frontier models without foreign hardware.

China can already run competitive AI models on domestic hardware, but it still has not demonstrated a frontier-scale training run using a fully domestic stack.

Frontier training requires thousands of accelerators to work together reliably at scale. That coordination depends on fast connections between chips, sufficient memory and stable software. A weakness anywhere in the system can stop the run.

China still relies on Nvidia stockpiles and approved imports for frontier training while Huawei develops domestic infrastructure around Ascend. Bringing that infrastructure to scale will also require more chip output from SMIC and continued progress in domestic memory and networking.

The 2027–28 model generation is the first that could plausibly be trained on Huawei’s domestic infrastructure. A fully disclosed training run would confirm that China can train frontier models without foreign hardware.

The Blokyz team brought me on to audit their contract, and when they asked me to be a signer on the multisig, I happily obliged.

2/3 multisig does not make the project rug-proof, but it does mean that any contract actions (like setting the raffle root, refundTotal, or withdrawing the proceeds) must be approved by myself or SimpleFarmer, in addition to the Blokyz team.

As for raffle fairness - the selection mechanism has already been finalized, and a hash of the file has been stored on the contract in advance (allocatorHash is set to 0x248c357ef216602dfb5381b5e1f680a6a5b002c39f620f9ec9e054b6bf08ca22).

Post raffle, the allocation script will be made public and anybody can verify that the script used matches the stored hash, and also produces the raffle results used by the team.

This does not reduce the centralization risk, but does hold the team accountable in retrospect: if anything was manipulated, it is easy to prove publicly.

I audit a lot of projects and my audits should never be seen as an endorsement of a protocol/project, but as it pertains to the workings of the contract itself, I am always happy to step in and clear things up.

Good luck.
